articles_and_episodes.title: The 2026 General Election Result
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Dr Muriel Newman New Zealand’s 2026 General Election is done and dusted, but the outcome is too close to call. We won’t actually know who won until the special votes are tallied and the final result released by the Electoral Commission on Friday, 27 November. Of the 2,432,403 votes that were counted on election night, Labour won 29.36 percent of the party vote up from 26.91 percent in 2023, National won 29.21 percent down from 38.08%, the Greens won 13.3% up from 11.6%, ACT won 10.92% up from 8.64%, NZ First won 9.78% up from 6.08%, Opportunity won 5.96% up from 2.22%, and the Maori Party won 0.57% down from 3.08%. Combining party votes with electorate wins gives National 42 electorate seats in Parliament (an overhang of seven); Labour 36 seats (21 electorate and 15 list); the Greens 16 seats (two electorate and 14 list); ACT 13 seats (one electorate and 12 list); NZ First 12 list seats; Opportunity seven list seats; and the Maori Party five electorate seats (an overhang of four). On those preliminary results, our Parliament will grow from 120 seats to 131 seats: an eleven-seat overhang – seven created by National and four by the Maori Party. articles_and_episodes.title: We Are Swimming In Electoral Fraud
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Nathan Smith The moment, the exact second, that the 2026 election showed a result, there were claims about voting fraud from the left. When I heard those noises, all I could think was: if only they knew… The term “electoral fraud” gets bandied about every time a country heads to the voting booths. Most of the time, it’s referring to ballot stuffing, mail-in votes, fake numbers, early calls for winners, media bias, voter intimidation and other garden-variety examples of corruption. Electoral fraud does happen, but most claims about it are usually sour grapes. Still, as the saying goes, if you’re not cheating, you’re not playing hard enough. But exactly how fraud occurs during an election loses all meaning when the system itself is fraudulent. I have two stories from two different friends that will show just how fraudulent our political system really is, and why every election result is illegitimate. The first story is a conversation I had with a friend about a month prior to the 2026 election. My friend has spent almost his entire life in New Zealand. articles_and_episodes.title: Clean up politics, but not ours
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Rodney Hide The Opportunity Party campaigned on cleaning up politics. It was one of their five non-negotiables. Their policy promised to “hard-wire honesty, transparency, and genuine public participation into our democracy.” Good on them. Who could be against that? Then they won seats, and we got to see how it works in practice. The Herald reports that two public servants sit on Opportunity’s policy committee. We don’t know who they are. The party won’t say. Before the election, leader Qiulae Wong said these two would help negotiate a coalition. Asked whether she would name them, she said the party “haven’t agreed as a team whether we would make that transparent.” Our “neutral” public service is now involved in running a political party, developing policy for the party, campaigning against the government, and negotiating an agreement to form a government. It’s no wonder the party of transparency hasn’t decided whether to be transparent. On her first day at Parliament, Wong was asked whether the two had told their employers about their party roles. articles_and_episodes.title: Experts gang up on the voters
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Rodney Hide Here’s a tip. Always be alarmed when experts gang up to sign a letter telling us what to do. If they had a good argument, one author would be enough. This week, 46 of them signed an open letter titled “Keep the ‘P’ in MMP”. It’s addressed to the new Parliament. And experts? Give me a break. It turns out that when the common people voted, they didn’t vote the way they should have. That’s funny. I thought democracy was about people voting as they choose, not as experts think they should. The letter complains of “a breakdown, both accidental and deliberately engineered, in the purpose of the party and electorate votes.” The purpose? Says who? Voters get two ticks, and they have every right to use them as they see fit. Many gave their party vote to one party, and their electorate vote to the local candidate they reckoned would do the best job, or the one most likely to beat the candidate they least wanted. That isn’t a breakdown. That’s people thinking. The experts don’t like it. articles_and_episodes.title: Heads We Win, Tails It’s Illegitimate
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Simon O’Connor There is a simple test of whether someone believes in democracy: do they still believe in it when they lose? We do not yet have the final result from this election. The Electoral Commission will release the official count next Friday (27 November), once around 400,000 special votes are added in. Yet already a chorus has decided something has gone badly wrong. Not with their campaigns, their policies or their leaders, but with our electoral system itself. Before I address these concerns, I think we should note a very key democratic principle: an election is legitimate not because it delivers the result you wanted, but because everyone agreed to the rules before a single vote was cast, and everyone accepts the outcome afterwards. articles_and_episodes.title: The Report She Didn’t Release
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Erid Crampton In September, Finance Minister Nicola Willis released an MBIE-commissioned Sense Partners report claiming that breaking Foodstuffs into two pieces could be wonderful. I had my doubts and published them in a short research note. That note is not nearly funny enough to highlight in the third slot of our Insights newsletter. But the report that Willis didn’t release, until Tom Raynel and Kate MacNamara at NZME obtained it, is very amusing. Reports that ministers do not proactively release are often far more fun than the ones they want you to see. I particularly love it when a consultancy goes a bit beyond its brief to look at the actual problem, rather than just work through the solution that the government seems to want. Coriolis did a lot of work for MBIE on the break-up option, but it put that option into context. Its first recommendation was direct: ‘STOP CAUSING INFLATION’. Coriolis pointed to rapid increases in the minimum wage and the Reserve Bank’s balance sheet blowing out, noting that after these things had occurred, ‘there was suddenly a problem with New Zealand food prices’.
